summary.text: A capsid is the protein shell of a virus, and it encloses the virus's genetic material.
Most viruses have a helical or icosahedral capsid, although some, such as bacteriophages, have more complicated structures.
Some viruses are enveloped, meaning the capsid is coated with a lipid membrane that it acquires from a cellular membrane of the host.

facts.label: Nucleocapsid
facts.value: The capsid and core together bear this name

facts.label: Icosahedral shape
facts.value: Twenty equilateral triangular faces, close to a sphere

facts.label: Foot-and-mouth capsid
facts.value: Faces made of three proteins, VP1 to VP3

items.prompt: A virologist sees a capsid with 20 triangular faces that nearly forms a ball. How is it described?

options.label: Helical, a shape like a spring
Icosahedral, a shape approximating a sphere
Enveloped, because of a lipid coat
Filamentous, like a loose thread

items.explain: The icosahedral shape has 20 equilateral triangular faces and approximates a sphere; the helical shape resembles a spring.

items.prompt: Some viruses wear an extra lipid coat over their protein shell. Where does that coat come from?

options.label: The virus builds it from scratch with its own genes
The capsid proteins themselves fold into it
The capsid takes it from a membrane of the host it infected
The host's immune cells attach it as a tag

items.explain: The envelope is acquired by the capsid from a cellular membrane in the host.

items.prompt: A virus has entered a cell and starts replicating. How does it get the new subunits for its capsids?

options.label: They are built using the cell's own protein-making machinery
They are carried in whole inside the infecting virus
The virus builds them in its own tiny factories
They are borrowed from the cell's wall

items.explain: New capsid subunits are synthesized using the protein biosynthesis mechanism of the host cell.

items.prompt: Why must a virus build a stable protein shell around its genes?

options.label: To give the virus the energy it needs to replicate
To make the particle larger than the cell it infects
To let the host's immune cells grab hold of it
To shield the genome from extremes of pH or temperature and from enzymes

items.explain: The shell protects the genome from lethal chemical and physical agents, including extremes of pH or temperature and proteolytic and nucleolytic enzymes.

items.prompt: Some complex viruses with double-stranded DNA assemble an empty shell first. How does the DNA get inside?

options.label: Through a specialized portal at one vertex of the shell
The shell is built around the DNA as the proteins co-assemble
The DNA seeps in through gaps between the shell proteins
The shell dissolves and re-forms around the DNA

items.explain: Such viruses assemble empty procapsids with a specialized portal structure at one vertex, and the viral DNA is translocated in through it.

items.prompt: A farmer's plants carry a rod-shaped, filamentous virus. Which capsid symmetry do many such plant viruses have?

options.label: Icosahedral symmetry
A cylinder with a cap at either end
Helical symmetry
No symmetry at all

items.explain: Many rod-shaped and filamentous plant viruses have capsids with helical symmetry.

paragraphs.heading: A protein shell
paragraphs.text: A capsid is the shell of protein around a virus's genetic material. It is built from repeating protein units called protomers. The units you can actually make out in its 3-D shape are called capsomeres, and they may or may not match single proteins. The proteins themselves are called capsid proteins, or viral coat proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Core and envelope
paragraphs.text: The genome inside the capsid, sometimes with a core protein, is called the virus core, and capsid plus core together make the nucleocapsid. In enveloped viruses the capsid is coated with a lipid membrane, the viral envelope. The capsid gets this envelope from one of the host cell's membranes, such as the inner nuclear membrane, the Golgi membrane or the cell's outer membrane.

paragraphs.heading: Two common shapes
paragraphs.text: Most capsids are either helical or icosahedral. An icosahedron has 20 equal triangular faces and comes close to a sphere, while a helical capsid is shaped like a spring that fills the space of a cylinder without being one. Many rod-shaped and threadlike plant viruses are helical, and the best understood is the tobacco mosaic virus. Each of its coat proteins binds three nucleotides of its RNA, with 16.33 protein units per turn. Some viruses, such as bacteriophages, have more complicated shapes.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the pieces
paragraphs.text: An icosahedral capsid is made of 12 pentamers plus 10(T − 1) hexamers, where the T-number reflects how large and complex the capsid is. Each face can be made of one protein or of several; the foot-and-mouth disease virus uses three, named VP1–3. The heads of bacteriophages are often elongated icosahedra: a cylinder with a cap at each end.

paragraphs.heading: Building a capsid
paragraphs.text: After a virus infects a cell and starts copying itself, the cell's own protein-making machinery builds new capsid pieces. In some viruses, including helical ones and especially those with RNA genomes, the capsid proteins assemble together with the genome. In others, especially complex viruses with double-stranded DNA, the proteins first build an empty procapsid with a special portal at one corner. The viral DNA is then moved into the capsid through that portal.

paragraphs.heading: Protecting and delivering
paragraphs.text: The shell has to be stable enough to guard the genome against harm, such as extremes of pH or temperature and enzymes that break down proteins and nucleic acids. In viruses without an envelope, the capsid itself may take part in contact with receptors on the host cell, which leads to it crossing the cell membrane and getting inside. The genome is then released either by the capsid coming apart in the cytoplasm or by being pushed through a portal straight into the nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Family trees from shells
paragraphs.text: The structure of the major capsid protein has been used to sort viruses into lineages. Bacteriophage PRD1, the algal virus PBCV-1, mimivirus and mammalian adenovirus share one lineage. Tailed double-stranded DNA bacteriophages and herpesviruses belong to another.
